text: Step 1 of the investigation plan, for real: seeing what's actually running against OverlookClinicalDB. Not guessing, not assuming — querying the dynamic management views that show exactly what's connected and exactly what's executing during the window both departments described.

Sessions and requests are not the same question. sys dot dm_exec_sessions is one row per connected session, whether or not anything is actively running — a connection can sit there for hours doing nothing. sys dot dm_exec_requests is narrower: one row per request that is actively executing this instant. That's the one that actually matters for what's slow right now.

This query joins sessions to connections, filtered to is_user_process equals 1 to drop SQL Server's own internal system sessions. What's left is real client traffic — the Billing application, the Scheduling application, anyone connected through SSMS. program_name is the fastest way to tell which department's traffic you're looking at without memorizing every login name.

This second query is the one that matters most. Filtering session_id greater than 50 excludes SQL Server's own internal sessions. blocking_session_id is worth watching closely — a non-zero value means this request isn't slow on its own, it's waiting on another session, which is a completely different problem from a genuinely slow query.

Run both of these during the mid-morning window and you'll see a realistic picture: Billing sessions, Scheduling sessions, and a handful of requests with unusually high total_elapsed_time. Those long-running requests are exactly what Lesson 4 narrows down to specific queries.
